items.title: Population

now_src.name: Census Bureau Vintage 2025, via Department of City Planning

items.text: The 2020 census counted 8,804,190 people, the most ever. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 219,561 below that.
items.method: The 2000 count is the decennial census total (P001001). The 2025 figure is the Census Bureau's Vintage 2025 estimate for July 1, 2025, as reproduced in the Department of City Planning's July 2026 population estimates table; the bureau's May 14, 2026 press release confirms New York City's 2024 to 2025 change. The 2020 census count of 8,804,190 is from the 2020 redistricting file (P1_001N).
items.confidence: High. Both figures are Census Bureau counts or estimates.

items.title: Racial and ethnic makeup
items.text: Non-Hispanic white residents, the largest group in both counts, fell below a third of the city. The Asian share rose from 9.7% to 15.6%, the Hispanic share from 27.0% to 28.3%; the non-Hispanic Black share fell from 24.5% to 20.2%.
items.method: Shares are computed from the census counts in the API responses: 2000, 2,801,267 non-Hispanic white of 8,008,278 (35.0%); 2020, 2,719,856 of 8,804,190 (30.9%). Asian: 780,229 to 1,373,502 (9.7% to 15.6%). Hispanic: 2,160,554 to 2,490,350. Non-Hispanic Black: 1,962,154 to 1,776,891. The 2020 census changed how race questions were coded, so the categories are close but not identical across the two counts.
items.confidence: High for the counts; the 2000 to 2020 race categories are not strictly comparable.

items.title: Children under 18
items.text: Children were 24.2% of the city in 2000 and 19.6% in 2024, a period in which the total population grew.
items.method: The 2000 figure is the sum of eight age cells from Summary File 1 (male and female, under 5, 5 to 9, 10 to 14 and 15 to 17): 276,635 + 286,155 + 270,582 + 157,253 + 264,243 + 274,960 + 260,234 + 150,207 = 1,940,269. The 2024 figure is the ACS 1-year profile estimate DP05_0019E, with its published share of 19.6%.
items.confidence: High. The 2000 total is a sum of published cells, not a single published number.

items.title: Adults with a bachelor's degree
items.now_label: 2024 American Community Survey, age 25 and over
items.text: Share of residents 25 and older holding a bachelor's degree or higher. Median household income went from $38,293 in 1999 to $81,228 in 2024, in dollars of each year.
items.method: 2000: Summary File 3 table P037, bachelor's, master's, professional and doctorate degrees for men (396,819 + 175,082 + 90,076 + 34,151) and women (437,739 + 222,074 + 66,573 + 24,319) = 1,446,833 of 5,276,946 people 25 and over, 27.4%. 2024: ACS 1-year profile DP02_0068PE. Income figures are Census 2000 P053001 and ACS 2024 DP03_0062E.
items.confidence: High. Same universe and definition in both.

items.title: Life expectancy at birth

then_src.name: NYC Health Department, Epi Research Report
then_src.quote: Over the past decade (2001–2010), overall LE at birth in NYC increased 3 years from 77.9 to 80.9 years.

now_src.name: NYC Health Department, Nov. 20, 2025 release
now_src.quote: This has surpassed the high of 82.6 years from 2019 and 2023.

items.text: The Health Department's provisional figure for 2024 is 83.2 years. The final 2023 figure is shown.
items.method: The 2001 figure is from the Health Department's Epi Research Report on life expectancy (PDF text extracted locally; the report's own series begins at 77.9 for 2001 and is corroborated by the Mayor's Office chart PDF of Dec. 11, 2012 and a PubMed abstract). The 2023 figure is the final value cited in the department's Nov. 20, 2025 press release, which also reports a provisional 83.2 for 2024.
items.confidence: High.

items.title: Workers who work from home
items.now_label: 2024 American Community Survey, workers 16 and over
items.text: 92,151 workers in 2000 and 509,852 in 2024. The share commuting by public transit went from 52.8% to 48.7%.
items.method: 2000: Summary File 3 table P030, 'Worked at home' 92,151 of 3,192,070 workers 16 and over (2.9%); public transportation 1,684,850 (52.8%). 2024: ACS 1-year profile DP03_0024PE (worked from home) and DP03_0021PE (public transportation), both of workers 16 and over. Both surveys ask about the usual means of travel to work in the reference week.
items.confidence: High. Same universe and question in both.

items.title: Average Wall Street bonus

then_src.name: New York State Comptroller, bonus chart

now_src.name: New York State Comptroller, March 2026
now_src.quote: Wall Street's securities industry bonus pool reached a record $49.2 billion in 2025, up 9% from the previous year

items.text: The bonus pool for the city's securities industry was $13.0 billion in 2001 and $49.2 billion in 2025. Securities-industry employment was 198,200 in 2025, down from a 30-year high of 201,500 in 2024.
items.method: The 2001 row of the State Comptroller's Wall Street bonus chart reads '2001 13.0 -33% 74,100 -26%' (pool in billions, change, average bonus, change). The 2025 figures are from the comptroller's March 2026 release. Not adjusted for inflation.
items.confidence: High.

items.title: Median rent
items.then_label: 2002 Housing and Vacancy Survey, contract rent

then_src.name: NYC Housing Preservation and Development, 2002 HVS selected initial findings
then_src.quote: In 2002, the median monthly gross rent, which includes utility payments, was $788, while the median monthly contract rent, which excludes tenant payments for utilities, was $706 (Table 11).

items.now_label: 2023 Housing and Vacancy Survey, contract rent

now_src.name: NYC Housing Preservation and Development, 2023 HVS selected initial findings
now_src.quote: In 2023, the median monthly rent for all renter-occupied units was $1,641.

items.text: Contract rent, which excludes utilities, for all renter-occupied units. The rental vacancy rate was 2.94% in 2002 and 1.4% in 2023, the lowest since the survey began in 1968.
items.method: Both figures are the median monthly contract rent for all renter-occupied units in the Housing and Vacancy Survey's selected initial findings: Table 11 of the 2002 report and Table 6 (citywide, 2023) of the 2023 report, whose text calls it 'the median monthly rent for all renter-occupied units'. The 2002 median gross rent, including utilities, was $788. Not adjusted for inflation.
items.confidence: High. Same survey, same rent definition.

items.title: Visitors

then_src.name: NBC News, citing NYC & Company (2003)
then_src.quote: Last year, 35.3 million domestic and international visitors spent $21 billion, supporting 226,100 jobs and producing $731 million in tax revenues for the city, NYC & Company said.

now_src.name: NYC Tourism + Conventions, March 2026
now_src.quote: Total visitation grew modestly to 65 million visitors, up 0.7% over 2024

items.text: Domestic and international visitors combined. The record before the attacks was 37.4 million in 2000. International visitors were 12.5 million of the 2025 total.
items.method: The 2002 count is the closest full-year figure with a fetched source; NYC & Company's 2003 statement put 2002 at 35.3 million, up 0.3% from 2001, which implies about 35.2 million for 2001. The 2025 count is from NYC Tourism + Conventions' annual report release.
items.confidence: Medium for the early figure, which comes from a news report of the tourism agency's number. High for 2025.

items.title: City budget

then_src.name: NYC Office of Management and Budget, Message of the Mayor, fiscal 2002 executive budget
then_src.quote: The 2002 Executive Budget is $39.5 billion, a decrease of $1.0 billion from the forecasted results for 2001.

now_src.name: New York City Council, June 30, 2026
now_src.quote: $125.8 billion budget for Fiscal Year (FY) 2027

items.text: Total spending, all funds, in dollars of each year.
items.method: The fiscal 2002 figure is the total stated in the Message of the Mayor accompanying the executive budget released in April 2001, the last budget document before the attacks; the Council adopted the budget in June 2001 and the February 2002 financial plan later put fiscal 2002 spending at $41.3 billion. The fiscal 2027 figure is the Council's announcement of the adopted budget. Not adjusted for inflation.
items.confidence: High for both documents. The fiscal 2002 figure is the executive proposal rather than the adopted total.

then_src.name: Alliance for Downtown New York, State of Lower Manhattan 2011
then_src.quote:
Vacancy jumped from 4.8% in early 2001 to 13% in Q2

high of 13.7% in Q4 2004.

now_src.name: Alliance for Downtown New York, Q2 2026 real estate report
now_src.quote: Downtown's overall vacancy rate finished Q2 at 22.3%, unchanged from the first quarter and down 0.5% year-over-year.

items.text: Office inventory south of Canal Street is 82.3 million square feet. Employment below Chambers Street was 325,352 in 2001 and 282,009 in the first quarter of 2025.
items.method: Both vacancy rates are from the Alliance for Downtown New York: the 2011 State of Lower Manhattan report for early 2001 and the Q2 2026 real estate report. items.confidence: High for vacancy. Medium for the employment comparison.

items.title: Buildings 1,000 feet or taller

then_src.name: Wikipedia, list of tallest buildings in New York City
then_src.quote: In 1966, construction began on the World Trade Center complex, including twin supertall skyscrapers measuring 1,368 feet (417 m) and 1,362 feet (415.1 m) in height.

now_src.name: Wikipedia, list of tallest buildings in New York City

items.text: On Sept. 10, 2001 the four were the two towers, the Empire State Building and the Chrysler Building. One World Trade Center, at 1,776 feet, is the tallest of the 17 today.
items.method: Counted from the Wikipedia list of completed buildings by height: the twin towers (1,368 and 1,362 feet), the Empire State Building (1,250) and the Chrysler Building (1,046) in 2001; 17 completed buildings at or above 1,000 feet in 2026, with 520 Fifth Avenue topped out and not counted. The Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat database could not be fetched.
items.confidence: Medium. Source is a maintained encyclopedia list, not the tall-buildings council.

items.title: NYPD uniformed officers

then_src.name: Manhattan Institute, citing city data
then_src.quote: The city reached a high in police staffing at the turn of the millennium (Figure 7). In 2000, the city's 40,285 uniformed police officers represented a 49.7% increase over the 26,913 officers in 1980.

now_src.name: New York City Council, fiscal 2027 executive budget report
now_src.quote: Uniform Headcount            Fiscal 2026 Budgeted Full-Time Positions: 35,025        Fiscal 2027 Budgeted Full-Time Positions: 35,370  Actual Headcount as of April 2026: 34,497         Vacancy Rate as of April 2026: 1.5 percent

items.text: The City Comptroller's May 2002 audit put the peak headcount the federal crime bill required at 40,710. The fiscal 2027 budget funds 35,370 positions.
items.method: The 2000 peak is from a Manhattan Institute report drawing on city data; Vital City reported the FY2000 high as 40,280 and the City Comptroller's 2002 audit describes a required peak of 40,710. The April 2026 actual is from the Council Finance Division's report on the NYPD's fiscal 2027 executive budget.
items.confidence: Medium for 2000 (secondary sources, consistent with each other). High for 2026.

items.title: NYPD intelligence and counterterrorism budget

then_src.name: Mayor's Office, Jan. 16, 2002
then_src.quote: Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg and Police Commissioner Raymond W. Kelly today appointed United States Marine Lieutenant General Frank Libutti in the newly-created post of Deputy Commissioner of Counter-Terrorism.

now_src.name: New York City Council, fiscal 2027 executive budget report
now_src.quote: Intelligence and Counterterrorism  250,968   255,179   262,022   257,769   266,488   4,466

items.text: The post of deputy commissioner for counterterrorism was created on Jan. 16, 2002. Federal security and counterterrorism grants added $161.1 million in fiscal 2025 on top of the city-funded line.
items.method: The 'Intelligence and Counterterrorism' program area in the Council Finance Division's fiscal 2027 report: $266,488 thousand proposed for FY2027; FY2025 actual $255.2 million. The bureau's creation date is the Mayor's Office release appointing the first deputy commissioner. A separate 'Security/Counter-Terrorism Grants' area, federally funded, was $161.1 million in FY2025 actual spending.
items.confidence: High.

items.title: Federal homeland security grant to the New York City area

then_src.name: U.S. Office of Justice Programs, FY2004 UASI table
then_src.quote: Table 1. FY 2004 UASI Grant Program | Urban Area | State | Grant Award | Amount | (in millions) | Defined Urban Area* | Core County(ies)/ | Parish** | New York | NY | $47,007,064 | City of New York; Counties of | Nassau, Suffolk, and Westchester; | Port Authority of New York and New | Jersey

now_src.name: Gov. Hochul, Sept. 30, 2025 release
now_src.quote: Under the FY 2025 awards, New York is set to receive $22,069,395 in UASI funding, representing an 85.9 percent cut from 2024's award of $156,131,176.

items.text: Fiscal 2024 is the last year with an undisputed award. For fiscal 2025 FEMA listed $92.2 million but the state said only $22.1 million was issued; FEMA's fiscal 2026 allocation is $142.5 million. The fiscal 2003 supplemental gave the area $125 million.
items.method: Both figures are Urban Area Security Initiative awards to the New York urban area, which includes the city, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties and the Port Authority: fiscal 2004 from the Office of Justice Programs' award table ($47,007,064) and fiscal 2024 from the governor's Sept. 30, 2025 release ($156,131,176; the release's table puts the city's own share at $118,451,583). The fiscal 2025 dispute and fiscal 2026 target allocation ($142,481,143, FEMA notice of funding opportunity) are described in the caption. Amounts are nominal.
items.confidence: High for both documents.

items.title: Stop-and-frisk stops

then_src.name: New York Civil Liberties Union
then_src.quote: In 2002, 97,296 NYPD stops were recorded.

now_src.name: New York Civil Liberties Union
now_src.quote: In 2024, 25386 stops were recorded.

items.text: Stops peaked at 685,724 in 2011, before a federal court found the practice as applied unconstitutional in 2013.
items.method: Annual stop counts as compiled by the NYCLU from NYPD data. 2002 is the first year with published totals. No 2025 total had been posted as of Sept. 2026.
items.confidence: High.

items.title: People in city jails

then_src.name: Mayor's Management Report, fiscal 2002
then_src.quote: Average Daily Inmate Population vs. Average Systemwide Length of Stay 17,524 17,562 15,530 14,490 13,934 49 51 46 44 48

now_src.name: Mayor's Management Report, fiscal 2025
now_src.quote: average daily population (ADP) in Fiscal 2025 was 6,823, an increase of nearly 10 percent from Fiscal 2024.

items.text: Department of Correction custody, mostly on Rikers Island. The population bottomed at 4,961 in fiscal 2021 and has risen each year since.
items.method: Both figures are the Department of Correction's average daily population as reported in the Mayor's Management Report: the fiscal 2002 report's five-year chart (fiscal 1998 to 2002: 17,524; 17,562; 15,530; 14,490; 13,934) and the fiscal 2025 report's indicator table (fiscal 2021 to 2025: 4,961; 5,559; 5,873; 6,206; 6,823). Fiscal years end June 30, so fiscal 2001 ended two months before the attacks.
items.confidence: High. Same agency measure in the same report series.

now_src.name: CDC, WTC Health Program quarterly summary
now_src.quote: 5. Currently Enrolled Members by Type | # Members | 145,275 | 15,685 | 71,417 | 56,692 | June 30, 2026 | Enrollment Data Thru:

items.text: Of those enrolled, 67.3% are certified for at least one 9/11-related condition. The Victim Compensation Fund had awarded $18.56 billion on 112,302 claims as of Aug. 31, 2026.
items.method: Enrollment and certification share from the CDC's June 30, 2026 quarterly program summary. The compensation figures are from the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund's August 2026 monthly report.

items.title: FDNY members lost

then_src.name: FDNY, Dec. 9, 2025
then_src.quote: 343 FDNY members who made the Supreme Sacrifice

items.now_label: died since of World Trade Center illness, FDNY count

now_src.name: FDNY, Sept. 8, 2025
now_src.quote: The Department has lost more than 400 members to World Trade Center illnesses.

items.text: The NYPD lost 23 members on the day; its tribute page lists 469 who have since died of 9/11-related illness. The medical examiner has identified 1,654 of the 2,753 people killed in New York; 1,099 remain unidentified.
items.method: FDNY press releases of Sept. 8 and Dec. 9, 2025 state the 343 and 'more than 400' figures. Thirty-six more names were added to the FDNY memorial wall on Sept. 2, 2026. The NYPD figures are the 23 stated on its 9/11 tribute page and a count of the 469 names listed there as of Sept. 6, 2026. Identification figures are from the Aug. 24, 2026 Mayor's Office and medical examiner release.
items.confidence: High for FDNY. Medium for the NYPD 469, which is a count of names on the official page.

items.title: Murders
items.text: The seven major felonies together fell from 162,908 to 121,652. Felony assaults rose over the same period, from 23,453 to 29,838.
items.method: NYPD historical table of the seven major felony offenses, 2000 to 2025 (2025 as of Jan. 19, 2026). The 2001 murder count excludes the 9/11 victims, which the NYPD tallies separately. The NYPD's Jan. 6, 2026 release cited 305 murders for 2025; the table's later figure of 309 is used.
items.confidence: High.

items.title: Subway rides in a year

then_src.name: MTA 2001 annual report
then_src.quote: MTA New York City Transit ridership totaled 2.14 billion in 2001, the highest level since 1970. Subways carried 1.41 billion passengers, buses 739.5 million.

items.text: The MTA called 2001's total the highest since 1970. The base fare was $1.50 then and is $3 now. Citi Bike, which opened in 2013, carried more than 46 million rides in 2025.
items.method: 2001: the MTA's 2001 annual report ('Subways carried 1.41 billion passengers'). 2025: the MTA's ridership page, 1,281,883,362 annual rides, 4,001,735 average weekday. Fare figures from a 2003 Gotham Gazette report on the increase from $1.50 and the MTA's current fares page; Citi Bike figures from Lyft, the operator.
items.confidence: High for ridership. The 2001 fare figure is from a news source.

items.title: Airport passengers

now_src.name: Port Authority, Feb. 6, 2026 release
now_src.quote: JFK's 2025 volume of 62.6 million passengers was a 1.0 percent decrease from its 2024 record of 63.3 million. LGA's 2025 total of 32.8 million passengers declined 2.2 percent from its 2024 record of 33.5 million. ... Its 2025 total of 47 million passengers was 4.2 percent behind 2023 (49.08 million)

items.text: JFK went from 29.4 million passengers to 62.6 million, LaGuardia from 22.5 million to 32.8 million and Newark from 31.1 million to 47.0 million. All Port Authority airports together, including Stewart, handled 142.7 million in 2025.
items.method: 2001: table 2.4.1 of the Port Authority's 2003 airport traffic report, total 82,970,417 across JFK, Newark and LaGuardia (JFK 29,350,052; Newark 31,100,491; LaGuardia 22,519,874). 2025: the three airports' totals as stated in the Port Authority's Feb. 6, 2026 release (62.6 + 32.8 + 47.0 = 142.4 million), summed here so the comparison covers the same three airports; the release's systemwide total of 142.7 million also includes Stewart, which the Port Authority did not operate in 2001.
items.confidence: High.
